origin_region: Shizuoka · Makinohara, Kakegawa, Kawane, Honyama, Tenryū, Fujieda
cultivar: Yabukita (bred here), with Kōshun, Tsuyuhikari, Yamakai and Saemidori lots
processing: Steamed sencha in every style: deep-steamed (fukamushi) on the Makinohara plateau and around Kakegawa, light to normal steaming in the mountain districts of Kawane, Honyama and Tenryū; refined and fired by the prefecture's large tea trade, which also blends tea from other regions.
harvest_season: First flush from late April into mid-May (earlier on the coast, later in the mountains), second flush in late June, autumn bancha; the first flush is what the name is sold on.
appearance_dry: Dark green needles, short and broken with green dust in deep-steamed lots, long and glossy in mountain lots.
appearance_liquor: From opaque deep green (fukamushi) to clear pale gold-green (asamushi).
appearance_wet: Fine green paste or whole small leaves depending on the steaming.
taste_profile: The textbook sencha: fresh green, savoury and sweet with a balanced astringency; deep-steamed Makinohara lots are thick and mellow, mountain lots are high-aroma and brisk.

brewing.notes: Check whether your lot is deep-steamed (short steeps, fine mesh) or light-steamed (a longer first steep); 70–80 °C either way.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's harvest and graded by flush: ichibancha from late April, sold first as shincha and then as the year's sencha until the next spring, with nibancha going into cheaper blends and bottled tea. Shizuoka is also the country's blending hub, so a bag labelled 'Shizuoka tea' may be a blend finished there; single-district lots (Kawane, Honyama, Kakegawa) state the district. Not an ageing tea.
description:
Shizuoka, the prefecture under Mount Fuji, has been Japan's biggest tea producer for more than a century and still grows roughly a third of the crop, with Kagoshima now hard on its heels. Its tea is sencha in every style the country makes, from the thick, cloudy deep-steamed teas of the Makinohara plateau and Kakegawa to the clear, aromatic mountain teas of Kawane, Honyama and the Tenryū valley, and the Yabukita cultivar that dominates Japanese tea was selected here.

The plateau tea is the volume tea: the Makinohara plateau was opened for tea by former samurai after the Meiji restoration, and its flat, sunny fields grow thick leaves that the local processors learned to tame with long steaming, which is how fukamushi was born. Up the Ōi and Abe rivers the story is different, with small terraced gardens, slow-growing leaf and short steaming that keeps whole needles and high aroma. Shizuoka is also the national trading and blending hub, so a great deal of tea from other prefectures passes through its refineries and comes out labelled Shizuoka.

Check which style you have before you brew. Deep-steamed Kakegawa or Makinohara lots want 30–40 seconds at 75 °C and a fine mesh; Kawane or Honyama lots want a full minute or more and a standard kyusu. Either way the profile is the textbook sencha: fresh green, savoury, sweet after the swallow, with a balanced astringency, thick and mellow in the coastal teas and lifted and brisk in the mountain ones.

Shizuoka-cha on its own usually means a blend finished in the prefecture, which is often very good and very consistent; single-district lots name the district (Kakegawa, Kawane, Honyama, Tenryū, Umegashima) and cost more. The harvest calendar runs from late April on the coast to mid-May in the mountains, shincha first, then the year's ichibancha, with second flush going to cheap blends and bottled tea. Beyond Yabukita, look for Kōshun, Tsuyuhikari and Yamakai as the local cultivars worth trying.

Buy a coastal fukamushi and a mountain asamushi from the same spring and you have the full range of Japanese sencha in two bags.
sources_note: Production share ('roughly a third') is approximate; Shizuoka and Kagoshima have traded the top spot in recent statistics.
